weathergenr

Stochastic weather generation for water resources and climate risk assessment.

weathergenr is an R package for generating alternative daily precipitation and temperature sequences from historical weather data. Use these sequences as inputs to hydrological and water-resources models to explore how climate variability and changing climate conditions affect your system.

What can you use it for?

  • Explore how different sequences of wet and dry years affect streamflow, storage and water supply.
  • Test a system’s sensitivity to changes in precipitation, temperature and other climate characteristics.
  • Compare adaptation options across many possible weather sequences.

The package supports gridded data, multiple weather variables and NetCDF input and output. It includes diagnostics for comparing generated weather with the historical record.

How it works

The generator combines year-to-year climate variability with daily weather resampling. It is designed to represent seasonality, wet and dry spells, and relationships between variables and locations. Generated sequences provide alternative realizations of climate variability; they are not forecasts.

For climate stress testing, first generate and evaluate weather under historical conditions. Then apply controlled climate changes in a separate perturbation step. This lets you explore conditions that would challenge a water system without tying the assessment to a single climate projection.

Get started

Install from GitHub in R:

install.packages("remotes")  # Once, if needed
remotes::install_github("Deltares-research/weathergenr")

Start with the worked example, which uses the included ERA5 dataset for the Ntoum Basin in Gabon. It walks through reading weather data, generating sequences and evaluating the results.

A typical workflow is:

  1. Prepare historical data. Supply daily precipitation and temperature for your study area. The package uses a 365-day calendar, excluding 29 February.
  2. Generate an ensemble. Create multiple weather sequences with run_weather_generator().
  3. Evaluate the results. Check the statistics and diagnostics that matter for your application, including seasonality, spell lengths and spatial relationships.
  4. Build climate change scenarios. Use apply_climate_perturbations() to change the generated climate, then run your impact model to assess system performance.

The quality of the historical data and the generator’s fit to your catchment matter. Review the diagnostics before using an ensemble for decisions, especially where drought persistence or extremes drive the outcome.

Documentation

  • Getting started — a worked generation and evaluation example.
  • Climate perturbations — setting up climate stress scenarios and their required inputs.
  • Function reference — arguments, data formats and available tools.

Method and citation

The package adapts the weather-generation framework of Steinschneider and Brown (2013) for gridded datasets and NetCDF workflows:

Steinschneider, S., & Brown, C. (2013). A semiparametric multivariate, multisite weather generator with low-frequency variability for use in climate risk assessments. Water Resources Research, 49(11), 7205–7220. doi:10.1002/wrcr.20528
